digest.top_line: SMART-KEY: cisplatin-free induction → IMRT + pembrolizumab gives 2y LFS 65.1% in stage III–IVB glottic/supraglottic SCC, matching RTOG 9111's 64.9% cross-trial; single-arm, N=43.
digest.tldr: Head and neck carried the day: larynx preservation without cisplatin (SMART-KEY), on-CRT ctDNA clearance tracking EFS in HPV- LA HNSCC (KEYNOTE-412), and neoadjuvant NivoDP MPR 60.9% in node-positive high-grade SGC, all single-arm or retrospective. APCCC 2026 reached consensus on 44 of 134 high-risk/locally advanced PC questions, none on fractionation. RADIANT: external LC/LRC C-index 0.76-0.86.

sites.intro: Four LA HNSCC/SGC reads, all IO-layered around CRT or surgery; none isolates RT's contribution, and RT dose/volumes are missing from two of the four (SMART-KEY, NivoDP).

studies.name: GORTEC 2024-03 IDEAL
studies.tldr: Interim safety: G3 TEAEs in 6 vs 2 of 10 pts per arm, no G4; preliminary post-induction ORR 71% (first 15 evaluable) before 70 Gy IMRT-cisplatin.
details: 🔍 Randomized (1:1) phase II, LA-HNSCC: larynx, hypopharynx, oral cavity, oropharynx (p16- and p16+)
💊 Arm A: induction pucotenlimab 200 mg + becotatug vedotin 2.3 mg/kg Q3W ×3 → CRT → adjuvant pucotenlimab Q3W ×8
💊 Arm B: induction becotatug vedotin (EGFR-ADC) alone → CRT, no adjuvant IO
🔍 CRT backbone: IMRT 70 Gy + concurrent cisplatin, identical in both arms
🔍 Primary endpoint: CR at 12 wk post-CRT; each arm tested independently (one-stage Fleming, H0=30%), 106 pts planned
🔍 49 randomized Oct 2025 to Apr 2026; 31 oropharynx, 19 of them p16+

details.text: 📊 First interim safety analysis (after cycle 1, first 20 pts)
📊 G3 TEAEs by arm (11 events in 8 pts)
subdetails: Arm A: ALT increase + constipation (1), myalgia + ALT increase + hypertension (1), neutropenia (1), diabetes (1), diarrhea (1), hyponatremia (1)
Arm B: peripheral arterial ischemia (1), fatigue (1)

details: 📊 ORR (RECIST 1.1) after induction 71% in first 15 evaluable pts; not split by arm, immature
⚠️ Primary endpoint (12-wk post-CRT CR) not yet reported; no CRT compliance or RT-phase toxicity data in source
⚠️ Safety read is cycle 1 only, 10 pts per arm; non-comparative design cannot isolate the PD-1 contribution

verdict.rationale: First interim safety analysis after one cycle in 20 pts; primary CR endpoint unreported, ORR pooled and immature, arms tested non-comparatively.
verdict.audience: LA-HNSCC (larynx, hypopharynx, oral cavity, oropharynx p16- and p16+)

studies.significance: The RT question is whether three cycles of EGFR-ADC induction compromise delivery of 70 Gy IMRT with concurrent cisplatin, and the source gives no CRT-phase compliance or toxicity data yet. The 12-wk post-CRT CR primary endpoint will be the first read on whether induction adds to definitive CRT response.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: **Randomized (1:1) phase II**, two arms each evaluated independently by one-stage Fleming design against **H0=30%**. 106 pts planned; 49 randomized between October 2025 and April 2026.

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: **LA-HNSCC** of the larynx, hypopharynx, oral cavity and oropharynx, **p16- and p16+**. Oropharynx dominated (31 pts, 19 p16+).

analysis_sections.label: Regimen
analysis_sections.body: Arm A: **pucotenlimab 200 mg + becotatug vedotin 2.3 mg/kg Q3W ×3**, then CRT, then adjuvant pucotenlimab Q3W ×8. Arm B: induction ADC alone, then CRT.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: **IMRT 70 Gy with concurrent cisplatin** in both arms. Fractionation and target volumes not stated in source.

analysis_sections.label: Endpoints
analysis_sections.body: **Primary: CR at 12 weeks post-CRT.** Post-induction ORR per RECIST 1.1 also reported.

analysis_sections.label: Safety
analysis_sections.body: After cycle 1 in 20 pts, **no G4 AEs**; 11 G3 TEAEs in 8 pts (**6 arm A, 2 arm B**). One arm B death post-gastrostomy after one ADC cycle, deemed unrelated.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: The stated rationale is MRG003 ± HX008 activity in R/M HNSCC (Xue, Clin Cancer Res 2026). Moving an EGFR-ADC and anti-PD-1 into induction before standard cisplatin-CRT tests that signal in curative-intent disease, where induction strategies have yet to displace definitive CRT.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents fit LA-HNSCC pts eligible for cisplatin-based CRT, p16- and p16+ oropharynx included. Does not represent R/M disease, nasopharynx, or cisplatin-ineligible pts.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: More G3 events in the IO arm after a single cycle; cumulative toxicity across three induction cycles and into CRT is unknown. The pooled ORR cannot be attributed to either arm, and p16+ and p16- disease are mixed.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: The abstract establishes only that cycle-1 toxicity is manageable. Whether induction ADC ± PD-1 improves CR after CRT, or delays or degrades RT delivery, is unsettled until the primary endpoint and CRT compliance are reported.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: Both arms carry 70 Gy IMRT with concurrent cisplatin after three induction cycles, so the RT read is whether ADC induction delays or degrades CRT delivery. The source reports no CRT compliance or RT-phase toxicity yet, and the 12-wk post-CRT CR endpoint will be the first test of added response.
significance_by_specialty.medonc: The IO + ADC arm had G3 TEAEs in 6 of 10 pts vs 2 of 10 with ADC alone after cycle 1, mostly hepatic, metabolic and GI. The 71% ORR is pooled across arms, so the PD-1 contribution in induction is not yet separable.

open_questions: Does induction EGFR-ADC compromise cisplatin-CRT delivery?
Does adding anti-PD-1 raise 12-wk post-CRT CR over ADC alone?
Is benefit different in p16+ vs p16- oropharynx?

studies.name: Neoadjuvant NivoDP in High-grade Salivary Gland Carcinoma
studies.tldr: MPR 60.9% and pCR 32.6% in 46 operated pts with node-positive high-grade SGC, above the MPR ≥50% threshold; 24-mo DFS 76.0%.
details: 🔍 Phase II, single-center, single-arm; 55 enrolled, 50 analyzed
💊 Nivolumab 360 mg + docetaxel 60 mg/m2 + cisplatin 60 mg/m2 q3w x3 → surgery → risk-adapted adjuvant RT
🔍 Treatment-naïve resectable high-grade SGC, clinically node-positive; stage III/IVA/IVB 34.0%/64.0%/2.0%
🔍 Salivary duct carcinoma 74.0% of cohort; 88.0% male
📊 ORR 52.0%; 46 pts (92.0%) reached surgery, R0 93.5%
⚠️ 4 not operated: 1 withdrawal, 2 progression, 1 G3 drug-induced pneumonitis
📊 12-/24-mo DFS 89.0%/76.0%; 24-mo OS 91.2%; median f/u 16.2 mo from surgery
📐 MPR vs non-MPR DFS: NR vs 24.2 mo, HR 0.19 (95% CI 0.05-0.71), p=0.013
⚠️ MPR-vs-non-MPR DFS is a responder comparison, prognostic not proof of treatment benefit
⚠️ Adjuvant RT dose, volumes and risk-adaptation criteria not reported in source

verdict.rationale: Single-arm, single-center phase II with a pathologic surrogate endpoint and 16.2-mo median follow-up; no randomized comparator vs upfront surgery plus adjuvant RT.
verdict.audience: Treatment-naïve resectable high-grade SGC, clinically node-positive

studies.significance: Adjuvant RT was risk-adapted after surgery, yet the abstract gives no dose, volume, or how a pCR (32.6% of operated pts) changed the RT plan. That leaves the de-escalation question open: whether pCR after NivoDP can justify reduced or omitted adjuvant RT in node-positive SGC is untested here.
studies.monday_clinic: In node-positive high-grade SGC, especially salivary duct carcinoma, this supports discussing a neoadjuvant chemo-IO trial before resection; it does not establish a survival benefit over upfront surgery plus adjuvant RT, nor any change to adjuvant RT dosing.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: **Phase II, single-center, single-arm**; 55 enrolled, 4 screen failures and 1 benign histology excluded, **50 analyzed**. Median follow-up 16.2 mo (95% CI 12.0-20.1) from surgery.

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: **Treatment-naïve resectable high-grade SGC with clinically positive nodes**. Median age 62, 88.0% male, ECOG 1 in 88.0%; salivary duct carcinoma 74.0%, adenocarcinoma 10.0%, mucoepidermoid 8.0%.

analysis_sections.label: Regimen
analysis_sections.body: Nivolumab 360 mg + docetaxel 60 mg/m2 + cisplatin 60 mg/m2 q3w for **3 cycles**, then curative surgery.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: **Risk-adapted adjuvant RT** after surgery. Dose, fractionation, target volume and the risk criteria are not reported in source.

analysis_sections.label: Endpoints
analysis_sections.body: **Primary: major pathologic response** (≤10% viable tumor), threshold MPR ≥50%. Also ORR, R0, pCR, DFS, OS, safety.

analysis_sections.label: Results
analysis_sections.body: **MPR 60.9%** (n=28) and **pCR 32.6%** (n=15) among 46 operated, exceeding threshold. 24-mo DFS 76.0%, 24-mo OS 91.2%; MPR pts had longer DFS, **HR 0.19** (95% CI 0.05-0.71).

analysis_sections.label: Safety
analysis_sections.body: Mostly G1-2 TRAEs; **6 G≥3 TRAEs**, no treatment-related deaths. One G3 drug-induced pneumonitis prevented surgery.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: Current care for high-grade SGC is upfront resection plus adjuvant RT, with RTOG 1008 testing added concurrent chemo in the adjuvant setting. No randomized neoadjuvant data exist; this is the first chemo-IO induction signal in this population.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents treatment-naïve, resectable, clinically node-positive high-grade SGC, predominantly salivary duct carcinoma. Does not represent node-negative, low-grade, unresectable, or recurrent/metastatic SGC.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: Cohort is three-quarters salivary duct carcinoma, so subtype MPR/pCR estimates for other histologies rest on very few pts. Follow-up measured from surgery excludes pts who never reached it.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: High MPR and pCR show the regimen is active, but whether induction improves DFS over upfront surgery plus RT, or permits RT de-escalation after pCR, is unanswered. MPR's DFS association is prognostic, not evidence that inducing MPR changes outcome.

studies.interpretation:
High-grade salivary gland carcinoma with clinical nodal disease has long been managed by resection followed by adjuvant radiotherapy, with concurrent chemotherapy explored in the adjuvant setting (RTOG 1008), and distant failure remains the dominant problem. This trial moves systemic therapy to the front of the sequence. That order is the right one for a disease whose failure pattern is distant: it treats micrometastatic disease early, tests chemosensitivity in vivo, and leaves the local treatment unchanged. On those terms the activity is real. A major pathologic response in 60.9% of operated pts and pCR in 32.6% would be notable in squamous head and neck cancer, where the neoadjuvant immunotherapy programs (KEYNOTE-689 among them) have reported far less complete pathologic clearance with single-agent checkpoint blockade.

The confidence a reader places in it should be shaped by three design features. First, this is a single-center, single-arm phase II, so the comparator is a prespecified threshold, not a concurrent control. Exceeding MPR ≥50% shows the regimen is active. It says nothing about whether the regimen beats surgery plus adjuvant RT on any outcome that matters to pts. Second, the cohort is overwhelmingly salivary duct carcinoma (74.0%) and male, which fits SDC biology but means the striking pCR rates in adenocarcinoma and poorly differentiated carcinoma rest on a handful of pts each. Those subtype figures should be read as anecdote, not as a guide to which histology responds. Third, the DFS comparison by MPR status is a responder analysis. Pts who achieve MPR are selected for favorable biology, so a DFS HR of 0.19 tells you MPR is prognostic. It does not show that driving more pts into MPR would improve DFS.

The survival data are immature: median follow-up of 16.2 months, counted from surgery, so the four pts who never reached the operating room (two of them progressors) sit outside that clock. A 24-month DFS of 76.0% looks favorable, but without a matched control or longer follow-up it cannot be placed against historical surgery-first outcomes with any precision.

For the radiation oncologist, the main gap is that adjuvant RT is described only as risk-adapted. The abstract does not say how pathologic response modified dose, volume, or the decision to treat, which is the question a pCR rate of this size invites. If a third of node-positive high-grade SGC clears pathologically, the logical next trial asks whether those pts can safely receive reduced or omitted adjuvant RT. This study opens that question and does not answer it. Until a randomized trial against surgery-first sequencing reports, NivoDP is a reasonable trial option and an active regimen, not a new standard.

significance_by_specialty.medonc: First prospective chemo-IO neoadjuvant signal in high-grade SGC, driven by salivary duct carcinoma (MPR 67.6%). The 6 G≥3 TRAEs and one pneumonitis that blocked surgery are the safety cost against an ORR of 52.0%.
significance_by_specialty.surgonc: Neoadjuvant NivoDP did not compromise resectability: 92.0% reached surgery with R0 93.5%. Two pts progressed before surgery, so a short window of preoperative progression risk accompanies the response benefit.

open_questions: Does neoadjuvant NivoDP improve DFS vs upfront surgery plus adjuvant RT?
Can adjuvant RT be de-escalated after pCR?

studies.name: KEYNOTE-412 ctDNA analysis
studies.tldr: In HPV- LA HNSCC, ctDNA clearance at C3D1 linked to better EFS in both arms, OS only with pembro (P<0.001); HPV+ prognostic signal absent.
details: 🔍 Retrospective ctDNA analysis of phase 3 KEYNOTE-412: pembro or pbo + concurrent CRT, newly diagnosed unresected LA HNSCC
🔍 473 of 804 pts evaluable at both timepoints (pembro n = 233; pbo n = 240)
🔍 Tumor-informed Natera Signatera 16-plex assay; HPV status by p16
🔍 On-treatment draw at C3D1, in pts who completed 5 of 6-7 wk of CRT
📊 BL ctDNA positivity 95.6% HPV+ vs 95.3% HPV-
📊 BL ctDNA level correlated with BL target lesion size (Spearman ρ = 0.49 HPV-, 0.34 HPV+)

details.text: 📊 ctDNA clearance rate at C3D1, by arm and HPV status
📐 C3D1 ctDNA clearance vs outcome (P values; no HRs reported in source)

details: 📊 Higher BL ctDNA → worse OS (pembro arm) and worse EFS + OS (pbo arm) in HPV- pts (P < 0.05); no association in HPV+
⚠️ BL ctDNA prognostic value in HPV- was dependent on tumor size and stage, independent of ECOG PS
⚠️ No HRs, medians or absolute EFS/OS by ctDNA status in source; P values only
⚠️ Retrospective; evaluable subset only, and the C3D1 draw requires near-completed CRT (survivorship selection)

verdict.rationale: Retrospective biomarker analysis of an evaluable subset; association P values only, no effect sizes, and the BL signal depended on tumor size and stage.
verdict.audience: Newly diagnosed unresected LA HNSCC, definitive CRT ± pembro

studies.significance: The ctDNA draw sits at C3D1, after 5 of 6-7 wk of CRT, so clearance measures mostly the response to radiation and not a pretreatment selector. In HPV- disease clearance tracked EFS with or without pembro (P = 0.001, P = 0.011), which points toward on-treatment adaptive escalation. No effect sizes are reported, so it cannot yet set a threshold.
studies.monday_clinic: In unresected HPV- LA HNSCC on definitive CRT, this frames a late-CRT ctDNA result as prognostic context for EFS; it does not support ctDNA-guided de-escalation in HPV+ (p16+) disease, where BL ctDNA carried no prognostic association.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: **Retrospective** exploratory ctDNA analysis of the phase 3 KEYNOTE-412 trial (pembro vs pbo + concurrent CRT). Cox proportional hazards regression by arm and by HPV status (p16).

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: Newly diagnosed, **unresected LA HNSCC**. **473 of 804** pts had evaluable ctDNA at both BL and C3D1 (pembro n = 233, pbo n = 240). The C3D1 sample required completing 5 of 6-7 wk of CRT.

analysis_sections.label: Endpoints
analysis_sections.body: Association of BL ctDNA level and C3D1 ctDNA clearance with EFS and OS. Assay: tumor-informed **Signatera 16-plex**.

analysis_sections.label: Results
analysis_sections.body: BL positivity was near-universal (95.6% HPV+, 95.3% HPV-), so detection carries little signal and the **level** is what matters. Higher BL level predicted worse outcomes **only in HPV-** pts (P < 0.05), and that association depended on tumor size and stage.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: All pts received concurrent CRT. Dose and fractionation were not reported in the source. The on-treatment draw at **C3D1** falls late in the 6-7 wk course, so clearance reflects the response to CRT.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: KEYNOTE-412 and JAVELIN Head and Neck 100 both tested PD-(L)1 blockade added to definitive CRT in LA HNSCC. This analysis asks a biomarker question inside that setting and does not re-test the parent comparison.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents unresected LA HNSCC treated with definitive concurrent CRT, analyzed separately by p16 status. Does not represent resected (postoperative) disease or pts who did not complete most of CRT.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: Requiring the C3D1 sample excludes early progressors and pts who stopped CRT, which inflates clearance associations. Arm-specific P values (0.075 vs < 0.001) are not an interaction test, so the **pembro-specific OS link is unproven**.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: ctDNA appears prognostic in **HPV-** disease and, in the pbo arm only, clearance carried prognostic value in HPV+. The HPV+ discordance argues that one ctDNA rule will not cover both biologies. Clearance cutoffs and effect sizes are needed before this can drive adaptive trials.

studies.interpretation:
The most useful finding here concerns HPV- disease, and it is about level, not detection. Baseline positivity was essentially universal in both strata (95.6% and 95.3%), so a positive tumor-informed assay before CRT tells the clinician almost nothing in LA HNSCC. Baseline level was prognostic in HPV- pts, but the abstract concedes that this depended on tumor size and stage. Combined with the moderate correlation between baseline level and target lesion size (ρ 0.49 in HPV-), the honest reading is that baseline ctDNA mostly re-encodes tumor burden that staging and imaging already capture. It is not yet shown to add independent information.

The on-treatment signal is more interesting and more fragile. Clearance at C3D1 was measured after pts had completed 5 of 6-7 weeks of CRT. For a radiation oncologist, that makes it a near-end-of-treatment response marker for chemoradiation, not a pretreatment selector. Its association with EFS in HPV- pts in both arms (P = 0.001 with pembro, P = 0.011 with pbo) fits a model where residual ctDNA late in CRT marks radioresistant disease whatever the systemic partner. That is the logic behind adaptive designs that escalate therapy for persistent molecular disease, and this dataset lends it support. However, the requirement to have reached C3D1 builds in survivorship selection: pts who progressed early or could not finish CRT are missing, and conditioning on that tends to strengthen clearance-outcome associations.

The arm-specific OS story needs the most caution. In HPV- pts, clearance was associated with OS with pembro (P < 0.001) but not with pbo (P = 0.075). The authors frame this as a stronger link under pembro. But a significant P value in one arm and a non-significant one in the other is not evidence of effect modification, and no interaction test is reported. With roughly 230-240 pts per arm split further by HPV status, the difference may reflect power and event counts rather than biology. Pembro also raised clearance rates in both strata (72.6% vs 63.6% HPV-, 76.8% vs 62.7% HPV+). If more clearance did not translate into the outcomes the parent trial sought, then clearance is not a reliable surrogate for benefit from adding IO, which is a different question from whether it is prognostic.

The HPV+ result cuts against an assumption common in de-escalation thinking. Baseline level carried no prognostic association, and clearance mattered only in the pbo arm. For p16+ disease, where circulating tumor HPV DNA assays are already being studied, this abstract offers no support for a tumor-informed level as a selector for treatment reduction. The absence of HRs, medians, or clearance thresholds means none of these associations can yet be sized or applied. They are hypotheses for prospective, ctDNA-stratified trials, not tools for the clinic.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: Clearance is read at C3D1, after 5 of 6-7 wk of CRT, so it reflects the on-treatment response to radiation. In HPV- disease it tracked EFS in both arms (P = 0.001, P = 0.011), which supports end-of-CRT ctDNA as a candidate trigger for adaptive escalation trials. In HPV+ pts the BL level was not prognostic, which argues against ctDNA level alone as a de-escalation selector.
significance_by_specialty.medonc: Pembro raised C3D1 clearance in both HPV strata (72.6% vs 63.6% HPV-, 76.8% vs 62.7% HPV+). The clearance-OS link held only with pembro in HPV- pts (P < 0.001). That makes HPV- clearance under concurrent IO a candidate for selecting adjuvant IO intensification, pending effect sizes.

open_questions: Does late-CRT ctDNA persistence justify escalation in HPV- LA HNSCC?
Is clearance-OS association truly pembro-specific, absent an interaction test?
Can HPV+ disease use ctDNA kinetics for de-escalation?

studies.name: SMART-KEY (LACOG 0720)
studies.tldr: 2y laryngectomy-free survival 65.1% (80% CI 54.9-73.5) with cisplatin-free induction + IMRT/pembrolizumab, numerically similar to RTOG 9111's 64.9%.
details: 🔍 Single-arm, multicenter phase 2; N=43, 9 centers, enrolled Feb 2022 to Aug 2023
🔍 Newly diagnosed stage III–IVB glottic/supraglottic SCC; 62.8% glottic, 83.7% former/current smokers

subdetails: Induction: carboplatin AUC6 + paclitaxel 175 mg/m2 + pembrolizumab 200 mg, three 21-day cycles

details: ⚠️ RT dose, fractionation and target volumes not reported in source

details.text: 📊 2y outcomes vs historical controls (as tabulated by the investigators)

details: 📊 2y cumulative incidence: locoregional recurrence 18.8%, distant recurrence 7.4%
📊 G≥3 TRAEs 41.9%, one grade 5 event
📊 Immune-mediated G≥3 TRAEs 16.3%
⚠️ Comparison is cross-trial against historical controls; no concurrent randomised cisplatin-RT arm
⚠️ 80% CI on primary endpoint, N=43; the stated late-morbidity rationale is untested at 2y

verdict.rationale: Single-arm phase 2, N=43, 80% CI, comparison only to historical RTOG 9111 / GORTEC 2000-01 cohorts; late toxicity benefit, the core rationale, not yet measurable at 2y.
verdict.audience: Newly diagnosed stage III–IVB glottic/supraglottic SCC, larynx preservation

studies.significance: The concurrent phase was IMRT with pembrolizumab alone, and the 2y failure pattern is locoregional (18.8%) far more than distant (7.4%), so the open RT question is whether IO can substitute for cisplatin radiosensitization in-field. RT dose and volumes are not reported in source, which limits transfer to a given larynx-preservation protocol.
studies.monday_clinic: In newly diagnosed stage III–IVB glottic/supraglottic SCC, this does not displace cisplatin-based larynx preservation; it supports cisplatin-free IO-based organ preservation only as a question for randomised testing, and says nothing yet about late laryngeal function or late mortality.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: **Single-arm, multicenter phase 2**, 43 pts from 9 centers, enrolled Feb 2022 to Aug 2023. Presented as ESMO 2026 rapid oral 1537RO.

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: **Newly diagnosed stage III–IVB glottic/supraglottic SCC.** Median age 61.1y, 86% male, 62.8% glottic, 83.7% former/current smokers.

analysis_sections.label: Regimen
analysis_sections.body: Induction **carboplatin AUC6 + paclitaxel 175 mg/m2 + pembrolizumab 200 mg** x3 cycles, then IMRT with pembrolizumab, then **fourteen cycles of pembrolizumab** consolidation. No cisplatin at any phase.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: IMRT delivered with **pembrolizumab alone, no concurrent chemotherapy**. Dose, fractionation and target volumes not reported in source.

analysis_sections.label: Endpoints
analysis_sections.body: **Primary: 2y laryngectomy-free survival.** Also reported: larynx preservation, larynx dysfunction-free survival, OS, locoregional and distant recurrence, TRAEs.

analysis_sections.label: Safety
analysis_sections.body: **G≥3 TRAEs 41.9%** with one grade 5 event; immune-mediated G≥3 TRAEs 16.3%. Described by investigators as well tolerated despite that rate.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: Investigators benchmark against **RTOG 9111** (cisplatin+RT) and **GORTEC 2000-01** (TPF induction then RT). LFS 65.1% vs 64.9% and OS 74.4% vs 74% sit level with RTOG 9111; larynx preservation 86% vs 75.8% and dysfunction-free survival 83.7% vs 70.3% favor SMART-KEY over GORTEC 2000-01 cross-trial.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents newly diagnosed stage III–IVB glottic/supraglottic SCC treated on a larynx-preservation pathway. Does not represent other laryngeal subsites, recurrent disease, or pts managed with upfront laryngectomy.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: Historical comparators span different eras, staging and RT technique, so numerical parity is weak evidence of equivalence. The headline motivation, fewer late cisplatin/RT deaths, needs follow-up well past 2y, and G≥3 TRAEs of 41.9% temper the cisplatin-free tolerability claim.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: LFS appears limited more by death without laryngectomy (20.9%) than by laryngectomy itself, so the regimen's value will hinge on whether those deaths fall with time relative to cisplatin-RT. Locoregional failure (18.8%) is the dominant recurrence pattern, the axis a randomised trial vs cisplatin-RT would need to protect.

studies.interpretation:
The case for SMART-KEY is not that it beats cisplatin-based larynx preservation, but that it may match it while removing the drug most associated with late morbidity. The 2y numbers support parity, not superiority: LFS 65.1% against RTOG 9111's 64.9%, OS 74.4% against 74%, and larynx preservation 86% against 88%. The more favorable comparison is against GORTEC 2000-01, where larynx preservation 86% vs 75.8% and larynx dysfunction-free survival 83.7% vs 70.3% lean toward SMART-KEY, but these are cross-trial readings against a historical cohort assembled under different eras, staging conventions and RT technique.

The design limits what can be concluded. Forty-three pts with an 80% CI on the primary endpoint is a signal-finding trial, sized to rule out a clearly inferior result rather than to establish equivalence. Historical-control benchmarking in larynx preservation is especially fragile because selection drives outcome: performance status, T-category mix and nodal burden shift LFS more than most regimen changes do, and the source gives no T-stage distribution to check comparability. A favorable read requires that the 43 enrolled pts resemble the RTOG 9111 population, which the abstract cannot confirm.

The outcome breakdown is the most informative part. Deaths without laryngectomy account for 20.9% of pts, against 9.3% alive after laryngectomy and 4.7% dead after laryngectomy. LFS here is constrained by mortality more than by loss of the larynx, which matches the investigators' framing that non-cancer and late-treatment mortality is the problem to solve. Whether cisplatin-free therapy actually reduces that mortality is the claim the 2y data cannot test, since cisplatin-RT late effects accrue over years.

For the RT reader, the regimen replaces concurrent cisplatin with pembrolizumab during IMRT. Locoregional recurrence at 18.8% exceeds distant recurrence at 7.4%, so in-field control is where the regimen is tested hardest, and the absence of reported dose, fractionation and target volumes makes it hard to judge whether RT intensity was held constant relative to the historical arms. Toxicity also complicates the tolerability argument: G≥3 TRAEs of 41.9%, one grade 5 event, and 16.3% immune-mediated G≥3 events are not trivial, even if the late-toxicity profile turns out more favorable.

What would make this wrong: longer follow-up showing locoregional failures accumulating beyond the cisplatin-RT benchmark, or late immune or laryngeal toxicity eroding dysfunction-free survival. What would make it right is a randomised comparison against cisplatin-RT with late function and late mortality as co-primary concerns.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: IMRT ran with pembrolizumab alone, no concurrent cisplatin, and locoregional recurrence (18.8%) outpaced distant (7.4%) at 2y, so in-field control is the endpoint to watch. RT dose and volumes are not reported in source, which limits transfer to a specific larynx-preservation protocol.
significance_by_specialty.medonc: Carboplatin/paclitaxel/pembrolizumab induction plus a year of pembrolizumab consolidation matched RTOG 9111 LFS cross-trial without cisplatin. G≥3 TRAEs of 41.9% and immune-mediated G≥3 events of 16.3% mean cisplatin-free is not the same as low-toxicity.

Randomised comparison vs cisplatin-RT for larynx preservation
Durability of locoregional control without concurrent cisplatin

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: AI model development with a hold-out test set and independent validation in **retrospective and prospective cohorts** from China, the United States and the Netherlands. Pretraining on **119,782 RT cases from 14 centres**; hold-out test of **22,058 cases** from the 10 most prevalent tumour sites.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: Model inputs are planning CT, RT structure sets and **3D dose distributions**. Outputs cover GTV/CTV delineation and dose generation, plus downstream prediction from a frozen encoder with a generated-dose branch.

analysis_sections.label: Endpoints
analysis_sections.body: Segmentation scored by Dice, dose generation by ΔHI, ΔD98, ΔD2, ΔDmax and ΔDmean. Downstream heads covered **21 endpoints** in lung, oesophageal, rectal and cervical cancers: pCR/response, OS, PFS, LC and RT-related toxicities.

analysis_sections.label: Results
analysis_sections.body: Hold-out Dice **83.52% GTV** and **81.53% CTV**. Reported as outperforming baseline models, **particularly in external cohorts**; baseline figures not given in source.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: The comparison set out in the source is single-task AI tools trained in limited cohorts. The claimed advance is one pretrained encoder covering contouring, dose and outcome prediction, but without baseline numbers the size of the gain over those tools cannot be judged from the abstract.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents lung, oesophageal, rectal and cervical cancer RT for outcome and toxicity prediction, and the 10 most prevalent sites for contouring and dose. Does not represent tumour sites outside the hold-out set or prospective clinical deployment.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: Validation cohort sizes, how cases split between retrospective and prospective, and per-site Dice are not reported. Discrimination metrics alone say nothing about calibration or whether the predictions change plans or outcomes.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: The dose-aware toxicity heads are the most RT-actionable output, since pneumonitis and proctitis prediction from a full 3D dose map could individualise constraints. The abstract does not show that the model improves plans, contours or patient outcomes compared with current practice.

studies.interpretation:
RADIANT applies the foundation-model approach to radiotherapy: one encoder pretrained on a large multi-centre archive of planning CTs, structure sets and dose distributions, then adapted to contouring, dose generation and outcome prediction. The argument behind it is that RT departments already generate highly structured, spatially registered data, and that single-task models trained on one institution's cases waste most of it. The scale here, 119,782 pretraining cases from 14 centres and a 22,058-case hold-out, is what gives that argument weight. What the abstract can't yet show is whether the scale buys better clinical decisions or only better benchmark numbers.

The outputs vary in how ready they are. Contouring at overall Dice 83.52% for GTV and 81.53% for CTV is pooled across ten sites, and a pooled Dice hides the site-level spread that decides whether a physician can trust a contour. An 80s-range Dice can still contain a clinically consequential miss at a nodal boundary or a mucosal margin. Dose-generation errors are reported without units or a reference definition in the source, so they can't be read against a clinical tolerance. These outputs are best treated as workflow accelerators that still need full physician review.

The prediction heads matter more to a radiation oncologist. Radiation pneumonitis AUC 0.78-0.81 and rectal proctitis 0.84-0.85 come from a model that sees the whole 3D dose distribution, not a handful of DVH points, which is the input you would expect to beat conventional constraint-based models if spatial dose patterns carry information. The abstract reports that RADIANT beat baselines, particularly in external cohorts. Holding up under domain shift is the right test for this kind of model, but no baseline figures are given, so the size of the gain is unknown. Survival C-indices of 0.73-0.79 for OS and 0.76-0.86 for LC/LRC are respectable discrimination, but discrimination is not calibration. A model can rank pts correctly and still give absolute risks too far off to act on.

Several things would have to hold for this to change practice. Validation cohort sizes and the share of prospective cases need reporting. Calibration and decision-curve analyses need to show net benefit at clinically used thresholds. Most important, a prospective study would need to show that model-informed planning lowers toxicity or improves control compared with standard constraints. The Grad-CAM and transcriptomic findings are plausible-looking but exploratory, and they should not be taken as evidence that the model has learned biology. For now this is a capable research platform and a credible route to individualised dose constraints. It is not yet a clinical tool.

If calibrated, this bears on per-patient dose-constraint and OAR-sparing decisions; contours at Dice 83.52% GTV still need per-site review.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: Modified Delphi process: **144 international experts** drafted 313 multiple-choice questions, 134 on high-risk localised / locally advanced PC, PSA persistence and recurrence. **133 panellists** voted by web survey before the conference.

analysis_sections.label: Regimen

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: The intensification votes follow STAMPEDE over ENZARAD, whose null MFS (**HR 0.88**, 95% CI 0.67–1.15) came in a lower-risk population. ATLAS, PEACE-7, THUNDER and DASL-HiCaP are testing other ARPIs in this setting.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: 44 panellists abstained or declared themselves unqualified on fractionation, which shrinks the informed denominator. The Q6 vote against perioperative ADT + ARPI before RP **predates PROTEUS**, which was presented and published after the conference.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: The panel accepts RT and multimodal surgery as defensible for high-risk cN0 disease without settling the comparison. Its abiraterone-not-enzalutamide vote is drug-specific, not a class effect, and the ongoing ARPI trials will decide whether that distinction holds.

studies.interpretation:
For a radiation oncologist, this report is most useful where the panel split, not where it agreed. Only 44 of 134 questions crossed the prespecified 75% threshold. The questions closest to daily RT practice, treatment selection for high-risk cN0 disease and fractionation, both fell short of it. The 62–68% vote for RT plus long-term ADT ± ARPI over a multimodal surgical approach describes a field that treats both pathways as defensible, not one that has resolved the comparison. None of the evidence the authors cite tests RT against surgery directly in this population.

The intensification votes follow the trial evidence closely. A panel majority backs 2 yr abiraterone in very high-risk disease, and very few panellists voted for enzalutamide. That mirrors the split between STAMPEDE and ENZARAD. The authors point out that ENZARAD enrolled a lower-risk population (cN1 11% vs 39%, cT3–T4 47% vs 94%). Its null MFS result (HR 0.88, 95% CI 0.67–1.15) therefore does not cleanly test ARPI substitution in the population STAMPEDE treated. The panel is voting on drug-specific evidence, not a class effect, and that is defensible. ATLAS, PEACE-7, THUNDER and DASL-HiCaP will show whether the distinction holds, especially in pts without pelvic nodal disease. The ENZARAD signal in cN1 disease, or when pelvic RT is given for another reason, is preplanned but still a subgroup. It should not yet move practice on its own.

Fractionation is where a quick read of the vote misleads most. A combined 88% for some form of hypofractionation sounds decisive. But no single schedule reached consensus, and 44 panellists abstained or called themselves unqualified, so informed opinion is a smaller group than the headline suggests. The cited evidence supports caution on ultrahypofractionation for high-risk disease. HYPO-RT-PC had few high-risk pts, and the SHARP data are pooled from non-randomised prospective series. Moderate hypofractionation is presented as the established option. SBRT for high-risk localised disease remains a question for trials.

The focal boost discussion is the most transferable RT content. The authors describe a randomised trial in which an MRI-defined boost of up to 95 Gy on top of 77 Gy in 35 fractions improved bPFS and local failure, with no significant difference in late GU or GI toxicity. This makes dose escalation to the dominant lesion an option alongside conventional fractionation. How boost combines with moderate hypofractionation or SBRT is not addressed in the material provided.

The document generates no new outcome data. The authors say there was no formal literature review or meta-analysis, and the votes are distributions of expert opinion. One timing problem deserves attention. The consensus against perioperative ADT + ARPI before RP was reached before PROTEUS was presented and published. That trial reported a higher pCR or minimal residual disease rate and an MFS difference driven by PSMA-PET. So the Q6 vote reflects pre-PROTEUS opinion and may move when the question returns at the 2027 localised consensus conference.

papers.title: Management of Patients with High-risk Localised, Locally Advanced, and Biochemically Recurrent Prostate Cancer: Report from the 2026 Advanced Prostate Cancer Consensus Conference
RADIANT: A radiotherapy foundation model for treatment planning and outcome prediction across cancers
papers.abstract:
ESMO Congress 2026 abstract 170O · Proffered paper: AI and digital health · 2026-10-24 · presented by Zhen Zhang (Hangzhou, China)

Background: Radiotherapy generates structured planning CT, target/OAR contours and 3D dose maps, yet current AI tools are usually single-task models trained in limited cohorts. We developed RADIANT, a radiotherapy foundation model for an automated workflow from target delineation and dose generation to clinical risk prediction.
Methods: RADIANT used a 3D Swin Transformer encoder pretrained by masked autoencoding on 119,782 radiotherapy cases from 14 centres with paired planning CT, RT structure sets and 3D dose distributions. The encoder was refined with hierarchical GTV/CTV segmentation and dose generation. Outputs were tested in a hold-out set of 22,058 cases from the 10 most prevalent tumour sites. For downstream adaptation, a frozen RADIANT encoder was integrated with a generated-dose branch and task-specific heads for 21 endpoints across lung, oesophageal, rectal and cervical cancers. Validation included retrospective and prospective cohorts from China, the United States and the Netherlands, covering pCR/response, OS, PFS, LC and radiotherapy-related toxicities. Performance was compared with state-of-the-art baseline models.
Results: In hold-out testing, RADIANT achieved overall Dice scores of 83.52% for GTV and 81.53% for CTV, with dose-generation errors of 0.0695 for ΔHI, 0.0706 for ΔD98, 0.0129 for ΔD2, 0.0012 for ΔDmax and 0.0371 for ΔDmean. Across independent validations, RADIANT achieved AUCs of 0.72 for pCR after oesophageal nICT, 0.84 for rectal complete response, 0.78-0.81 for radiation pneumonitis, 0.84-0.85 for rectal radiation proctitis and 0.84 for cervical radiation proctitis. Survival models yielded external C-indices of 0.73-0.79 for OS, 0.71-0.78 for PFS and 0.76-0.86 for LC/LRC. RADIANT consistently outperformed baseline models, particularly in external cohorts. Grad-CAM highlighted clinically plausible tumour and normal-tissue dose interfaces; exploratory transcriptomic analyses suggested biological differences between model-defined risk groups.
Conclusions: Prospective and international multi-centre validation supports RADIANT as a scalable framework for AI-assisted radiotherapy workflows and decision-making.

papers.title: A phase II trial of neoadjuvant nivolumab, docetaxel, and cisplatin followed by surgery and radiation therapy for resectable high-grade salivary gland carcinoma
papers.abstract:
ESMO Congress 2026 abstract 1540RO · Rapid oral: Head and neck cancer · 2026-10-25 · presented by Sehhoon Park (Seoul, Republic of Korea) · NCT05727410

Background: Resectable high-grade salivary gland carcinoma (SGC) with clinical node metastasis carries a high risk of distant metastasis despite curative surgery and adjuvant radiotherapy, and effective neoadjuvant strategies remain undefined. We evaluated neoadjuvant nivolumab plus docetaxel and cisplatin (NivoDP) in this aggressive disease.
Methods: This phase II, single-center, single-arm trial enrolled treatment-naïve patients with resectable high-grade SGC and clinically positive lymph nodes. Patients received 3 cycles of nivolumab (360 mg) plus docetaxel (60 mg/m2) and cisplatin (60 mg/m2) q3w, followed by curative surgery and risk-adapted adjuvant radiotherapy. The primary endpoint was major pathologic response (MPR; ≤10% viable tumor).
Results: Of 55 enrolled, 4 screen failures and 1 with benign histology were excluded, leaving 50 analyzed (median age 62; 88.0% male; ECOG 0/1: 12.0%/88.0%). AJCC 8th stage was III/IVA/IVB in 34.0%/64.0%/2.0%. Salivary duct carcinoma predominated (74.0%), followed by adenocarcinoma (10.0%) and mucoepidermoid carcinoma (8.0%). ORR was 52.0%. Forty-six patients underwent surgery (92.0%); 4 did not (1 withdrawal, 2 progression, 1 G3 drug-induced pneumonitis). Among 46 operated patients, R0 resection was 93.5%, MPR 60.9% (n=28), and pCR 32.6% (n=15), exceeding the predefined threshold (MPR ≥50%). Among pathology subtypes, salivary duct carcinoma (MPR 67.6%, pCR 29.4%), adenocarcinoma (MPR 75.0%, pCR 75.0%), and poorly differentiated carcinoma (MPR 66.7%, pCR 66.7%) showed the best response to NivoDP. With a median follow-up of 16.2 months (95% CI 12.0–20.1) from surgery, 12- and 24-month DFS were 89.0% and 76.0%, and 24-month OS 91.2%. The MPR subgroup showed significantly longer DFS than non-MPR (NR vs 24.2 mo; HR 0.19, 95% CI 0.05–0.71, p=0.013). Most TRAEs were grade 1–2; 6 grade ≥3 TRAEs were observed, which were all manageable with no treatment-related deaths.
Conclusions: Neoadjuvant NivoDP showed promising clinical efficacy in node-positive high-grade SGC, with high MPR and pCR rates. MPR strongly predicted superior DFS. These results support neoadjuvant chemoimmunotherapy as a promising strategy in resectable high-grade SGC.
Clinical trial identification: NCT05727410.

papers.title: First interim safety analysis of GORTEC 2024-03 IDEAL: Randomized phase II trial of induction treatment anti–PD-1 pucotenlimab (HX008) plus EGFR-ADC (becotatug vedotin (MRG003) versus EGFR-ADC alone followed by chemoradiotherapy in locally advanced head and neck squamous cell carcinoma
papers.abstract:
ESMO Congress 2026 abstract 1538RO · Rapid oral: Head and neck cancer · 2026-10-25 · presented by Yungan Tao (Villejuif, France) · NCT06959108

Background: The EGFR-directed ADC becotatug vedotin (MRG003) alone or combined with anti-PD1 pucotenlimab (HX008) have shown promising efficacy along with a good safety profile in R/M HNSCC (Xue, Clin. Cancer Res. 2026). The IDEAL trial evaluates induction becotatug vedotin ± pucotenlimab prior to definitive chemoradiotherapy (CRT) in locally advanced (LA) HNSCC.
Methods: Patients (pts) with LA-HNSCC (larynx, hypopharynx, oral cavity, and oropharynx [p16 - and p16 +]) were randomized (1:1) to 2 arms: (A) induction pucotenlimab (200 mg) + becotatug vedotin (2.3 mg/kg) Q3W ×3 → CRT → adjuvant pucotenlimab (Q3W ×8), or (B) induction ADC alone → CRT. CRT consisted of IMRT (70 Gy) + concurrent cisplatin. Primary endpoint is complete response (CR) at 12 weeks post-CRT. Each arm is evaluated independently (one-stage Fleming design; H0=30%). A total of 106 pts is planned. The first interim safety analysis was conducted after completion of cycle 1 in first 20 pts.
Results: Between October 23rd 2025 and April 21st 2026, 49 pts were randomized. Most had oropharyngeal cancer (31 pts, including 19 p16 +). 20 patients (10 per arm) were evaluated for first safety analysis. One death occurred in Arm B (post-gastrostomy, after 1 cycle ADC), deemed unrelated to study treatment. No grade 4 adverse events (AEs) were observed in either arm. A total of 11 Grade 3 TEAEs were observed in 8 pts (6 arm A and 2 arm B). In arm A, these G3 TEAEs were ALT increase + constipation (1 pt), myalgia + ALT increase + hypertension (1), neutropenia (1), diabetes (1), diarrhea (1) and hyponatremia (1). In Arm B, G3 TEAEs were peripheral arterial ischemia (1) and fatigue (1). Data on ORR (per RECIST 1.1) after induction are preliminary and not mature, but ORR observed in 71% of first 15 evaluable pts. Updated safety and post-induction ORR data will be presented at the meeting along with preliminary results on primary endpoint.
Conclusions: First results of induction becotatug vedotin ± pucotenlimab in LA-SCCHN are encouraging and a favorable safety profile was observed.
Clinical trial identification: NCT06959108 First Submitted: 2025-04-28, EU CT 2023-510558-18-00.

papers.title: A single-arm, multi-institutional, phase 2 study of a pembrolizumab-based organ preservation strategy for locally advanced larynx cancers: SMART-KEY (LACOG 0720)
papers.abstract:
ESMO Congress 2026 abstract 1537RO · Rapid oral: Head and neck cancer · 2026-10-25 · presented by Thiago B. Oliveira (Sao Paulo, Brazil) · NCT04943445

Background: Standard larynx-preserving strategies yield similar laryngectomy-free survival (LFS) with no overall survival (OS) difference, but data raise concerns about late-onset toxicity and mortality, especially for concurrent cisplatin/radiation therapy (RT). We evaluated the addition of pembrolizumab to a cisplatin-free induction, concurrent and consolidation strategy for larynx-preservation.
Methods: This multicenter, single-arm phase 2 trial enrolled patients (pts) with newly diagnosed stage III–IVB glottic/supraglottic squamous cell carcinomas. Pts received induction carboplatin AUC6, paclitaxel 175 mg/m2, and pembrolizumab 200 mg (three 21-day cycles), followed by IMRT with pembrolizumab alone and fourteen 21-day cycles of pembrolizumab consolidation. Primary endpoint was two-year (2y) LFS.
Results: From Feb 2022 to Aug 2023, 43 pts from 9 centers were enrolled (median age 61.1y, 86% male, 74.4% White, 25.6% Black/Mixed, 83.7% former/current smokers, 62.8% glottic). The 2y LFS was 65.1% (80% CI: 54.9-73.5), which compares favorably with historical pivotal trials results. Additional outcomes are presented in the Table. Two-year cumulative incidence of locoregional and distant recurrence were 18.8% and 7.4%. Grade ≥3 treatment-related adverse events occurred in 41.9% pts (one pt with grade 5), with immune-mediated grade ≥3 TRAEs in 16.3%. Table: 1537RO Outcomes SMART-KEY Historical Control RTOG 9111 (Cisplatin+RT) Historical Control GORTEC 2000-01 (cisplatin, docetaxel, 5-fluorouracil/RT) 2y laryngectomy-free survival 65.1% 64.9% NE 2y larynx preservation rates 86% 88% 75.8% 2y larynx dysfunction-free survival 83.7% NE 70.3% 2y overall survival 74.4% 74% 73% Proportion of pts Alive with larynx 65.1% 64.9% NE Alive after laryngectomy 9.3% 9.1% NE Dead after laryngectomy 4.7% 2.9% NE Dead no laryngectomy 20.9% 23.1% NE
Conclusions: SMART-KEY demonstrated short-term oncological/functional outcomes numerically comparable to RTOG-9111 and potentially superior to GORTEC 2000-01, pivotal trials using cisplatin-based regimens. Our well-tolerated cisplatin-free, concurrent chemotherapy-free strategy also yielded low rates of distant recurrence. The long-term benefit of this regimen will be evaluated with additional follow-up but may have the potential to mitigate cisplatin/RT-related late morbidity/mortality.
Clinical trial identification: NCT04943445.

papers.title: ctDNA analysis of the phase 3 KEYNOTE-412 trial: Pembrolizumab (pembro) or placebo (pbo) + concurrent chemoradiotherapy (CRT) for locally advanced head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (LA HNSCC)
papers.abstract:
ESMO Congress 2026 abstract 1536RO · Rapid oral: Head and neck cancer · 2026-10-25 · presented by Jean-Pascal Machiels (Woluwe-Saint-Lambert, Belgium) · NCT03040999

Background: ctDNA is an emerging biomarker in multiple solid tumor types, but its value in LA HNSCC is unclear. KEYNOTE-412 (NCT03040999) evaluated pembro + CRT vs pbo + CRT in participants (pts) with newly diagnosed, unresected LA HNSCC. We retrospectively assessed the association of clinical outcomes with pretreatment ctDNA (baseline [BL] ctDNA) and early on-treatment ctDNA (cycle 3 day 1 [C3D1] ctDNA in pts who completed 5 of 6-7 wk of CRT) in KEYNOTE-412.
Methods: The tumor-informed Natera Signatera 16-plex assay was used to evaluate ctDNA levels in treated pts. Association of BL ctDNA levels and C3D1 ctDNA clearance with EFS and OS were assessed in each arm and by HPV status (by p16 testing) per Cox proportional hazards regression.
Results: Of 804 pts, 473 (pembro arm n = 233; pbo arm n = 240) had evaluable ctDNA samples at both BL and C3D1. BL ctDNA positivity rate was 95.6% for HPV+ and 95.3% for HPV- pts. BL ctDNA levels were positively correlated with BL target lesion size in both HPV- and HPV+ pts (Spearman ρ = 0.49 and 0.34, respectively). Higher BL ctDNA levels were associated with worse OS in the pembro arm and worse EFS and OS in the pbo arm in HPV- pts (P < 0.05); no associations in either arm were observed in HPV+ pts (P > 0.05). The association of BL ctDNA levels with outcomes in HPV- pts was independent of ECOG PS but dependent on tumor size and stage. ctDNA clearance rate at C3D1 was higher in the pembro arm (HPV- 72.6%; HPV+ 76.8%) vs pbo arm (HPV- 63.6%; HPV+ 62.7%). In HPV- pts, ctDNA clearance at C3D1 was associated with improved EFS in both arms (pembro P = 0.001; pbo P = 0.011) and with improved OS in the pembro arm (P < 0.001) but not in the pbo arm (P = 0.075). In HPV+ pts, ctDNA clearance at C3D1 was associated with improved EFS (P = 0.028) and OS (P = 0.013) only in the pbo arm.
Conclusions: The prognostic value of BL ctDNA was observed in HPV- pts with LA HNSCC but not in HPV+ pts. In HPV- pts, a stronger link between C3D1 ctDNA clearance and long-term survival was observed in the pembro arm. These findings suggest distinct ctDNA prognostic values in HNSCC based on HPV status, and long-term outcome associations may differ by treatment modality.
Clinical trial identification: NCT03040999.
